supportFile, pointing it at the cypress/api folder
specPattern in the config, for example 'cypress/api/**/*.cy.ts'
baseUrl, because Cypress looks for specs relative to the app address, not the file system

1ymjrnp.text: What does retries: { runMode: 2, openMode: 0 } mean?
options: Every command in a test is retried twice in run mode and never in open mode, regardless of assertions
Every test always runs twice in run mode and never in open mode
On CI at most 2 tests may fail

1cht6c6.text: What happens by default during cypress run in modern Cypress?

Neither screenshots nor video are taken

Turn on retries and close the ticket
Collect the artifacts (screenshot, video, logs), reproduce in the same Docker image and headless mode, check for dependence on data and timings

options: have.text ignores case
have.text ignores case, while contain compares character by character

1r9k4iq.text: How do you check several conditions for one element in a single chain?
options: `.should(['be.visible', 'have.class'])`
`cy.get('[data-cy=amount]').should(['be.visible', 'have.class', 'contain'], 'positive', 'PLN')`
`cy.get('[data-cy=amount]').should('be.visible').and('have.class', 'positive').and('contain', 'PLN')`
`.then(el => expect(...))` three times

12o11j0.text: What matters about the callback in `.should(($el) => { ... })`?
options: It runs exactly once, so you can call cy commands in it
The callback is repeated until it succeeds, so you must not call cy commands or cause side effects in it
It turns off the timeout

16k15lh.text: How do you check an input's value?

`cy.get('#amount').should('have.text', '100')`
`cy.get('#amount').invoke('text').should('eq', '100')`
`.invoke('text').should('eq', '100')`

Returns the text length of the first li and checks that it is at least 3 characters

meh147.text: How do you get an element's text for a later comparison?
options: `const text = cy.get('[data-cy=total]').text()`, then compare the string
`cy.get('[data-cy=total]').its('text').should('eq', expected)`
`await cy.get(...).text()`
`cy.get('[data-cy=total]').invoke('text').then(text => { ... })`

ft2g4v.text: How do you type text and press Enter?
options: `.type('playwright').submit()`
`cy.get('#search').type('playwright').enter()`
`.type('playwright\n')`
`cy.get('#search').type('playwright{enter}')`

gbc4uk.text: How do you clear a field before typing?

`cy.get('#amount').reset().type('250')`
gbc4uk.explanation: clear is a shortcut for `type('{selectall}{backspace}')`. Cypress has no fill command.

1tuzrlx.text: How do you pick an option in a `<select>`?

`.type('EUR')`
`cy.get('select#currency').check('EUR')`
`cy.get('select#currency').click().contains('EUR').click()`

1oe2xvy.text: How do you hover the mouse to show a menu that opens on mouseover?

ltm6fv.text: What does `{ force: true }` do in `.click()`?

Repeats the click until it succeeds, ignoring handler errors, and doesn't wait for animations
Skips the actionability checks, so the click works even on a covered or invisible element
Clicks faster by skipping the animation, but all the actionability checks stay

1k62l12.text: How do you upload a file to an input?
options: `cy.get('input[type=file]').type('cypress/fixtures/statement.csv')`
`.attachFile()` without plugins
`cy.get('input[type=file]').selectFile('cypress/fixtures/statement.csv')`
Cypress doesn't support file uploads

1foquvy.text: How do you limit a search to elements inside a form?

`cy.get('form#transfer').get('input[name=amount]').type('10')`
`cy.get('form#transfer > *').type('10')`
`cy.get('form#transfer').within(() => { cy.get('input[name=amount]').type('10') })`

1tk3gv5.text: How do you check the width of the mobile layout?
options: `cy.resize(375, 812)` before the actions
`cy.viewport('iphone-x')` or `cy.viewport(375, 812)` before the actions

q98o9k.text: How do you check that the /dashboard page opened after login?

`expect(window.location.pathname).to.eq('/dashboard')`

wjiqsd.explanation: Entry criteria are the conditions for starting (a ready build, environment, requirements). Without agreed exit criteria, the release decision turns into an argument.

options: The more tests you add to regression, the more bugs they find in each following release
The same tests repeated again and again stop finding new defects
Automated tests destroy manual testing
Fixing one bug creates another in a neighbouring module, so every fix needs a full regression
1alc3dm.explanation: The remedy: review and update cases regularly, add new data, use exploratory testing.

4knh1q.text: When is the decision table technique appropriate?
options: When the result depends on a combination of several conditions, for example a discount depends on customer status, amount and promo code
For checking the boundaries of a numeric field, for example the minimum and maximum transfer amount
For load testing
For testing transitions between order states, when it matters which statuses can follow each other and which transitions are forbidden
4knh1q.explanation: A decision table guarantees that no combination of conditions is missed. For states and transitions use state transition testing.

2dkgq2.text: A transfer has the statuses CREATED → PENDING → COMPLETED or FAILED. Which technique best covers the forbidden transitions?
options: Equivalence partitioning
State transition testing
Error guessing
Pairwise testing
2dkgq2.explanation: You build a state diagram, cover all allowed transitions and check the forbidden ones: for example COMPLETED → PENDING must be rejected.

1fpahzx.text: What does the testing pyramid state?
options: There should be the most E2E tests, because only they check the system the way the user sees it
Many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests, the fewest expensive E2E tests
Manual testing at the base of the pyramid, API tests above it, and unit tests at the top as the most expensive
All levels should have the same number of tests
1fpahzx.explanation: E2E tests are slow, brittle and expensive to maintain, so they cover the critical paths. An inverted pyramid (the "ice cream cone") is an antipattern.

options: Testing only the left part of the UI
Moving bugs to the next sprint
Moving testing to the end of the sprint, so you test already stable code
Involving testing as early as possible: requirement reviews, taking part in design, tests alongside the code
xqrzeg.explanation: A defect found in requirements is many times cheaper than the same defect in production.

1qn27jr.text: What is NOT needed in a bug report?
options: Steps to reproduce
Who QA thinks is to blame for the bug
Expected and actual result
Environment, build, evidence (screenshot, log, HAR)
1qn27jr.explanation: A bug report describes facts. A good title answers what broke, where and under what conditions.

qkbvju.text: How is an image different from a container?
options: An image is an immutable template, a container is a running instance of an image with its own state
A container is an immutable template with its own state, and an image is a running process that can be stopped and restarted
An image works only on Linux, and a container is its version for Windows and macOS with its own kernel
A container is an immutable template, an image is a running instance with its own state
qkbvju.explanation: Many containers can be started from one image. The analogy: a class and an object.

1vcc9yw.text: How is docker ps different from docker ps -a?
options: ps -a deletes stopped containers
ps -a shows images, and ps only the containers started from the current terminal
No difference
ps shows only running containers, ps -a shows all, including stopped ones
1vcc9yw.explanation: If a container has "disappeared", most often it crashed right after starting. Find it with ps -a and look at docker logs.

1sljrhb.text: What does -p 8080:80 mean in docker run?
options: The container uses both ports at the same time for HTTP and HTTPS
Host port 80 is forwarded to container port 8080
A limit of 8080 processes in the container and 80 open connections
Host port 8080 is forwarded to container port 80
1sljrhb.explanation: The format is host:container. From the browser you reach the service at localhost:8080.

1tw1ruu.text: The PostgreSQL container was deleted, and all the test data vanished. How do you avoid that?
options: Run the container with -it and don't close the terminal until testing is finished
Never stop the container and run docker commit after every run
Run docker commit after every test
Store the data in a volume that lives separately from the container
1tw1ruu.explanation: A container's file system is temporary. A named volume or a bind mount survives the container's removal.

1g4xq5.text: How is a Dockerfile different from docker-compose.yml?
options: A Dockerfile is needed only for Windows containers and docker-compose.yml for Linux; both describe how to run services, but with different syntax and commands
Compose builds an image from source code, while a Dockerfile runs ready containers and describes networks, ports and volumes
A Dockerfile describes how to build one image. Compose describes how to run several services together: networks, ports, volumes, variables
Compose describes how to build one image. A Dockerfile describes how to run several services together: networks, ports, volumes, variables
1g4xq5.explanation: A typical QA scenario: compose brings up the app, the database and mocks with a single docker compose up.

549lb6.text: How do you see what the application in a container has printed?
options: docker images --logs <image> for the right image
docker ps --logs
docker inspect <image> shows everything the application printed to stdout
docker logs <container> (with -f for streaming)
549lb6.explanation: The first step when a container crashes or a service returns 500. Attach the logs to the bug report.

1jjcys9.text: How do you run a command inside a running container, for example to open psql?
options: docker attach psql
docker exec -it <container> psql -U postgres
docker run -it <container> psql -U postgres
docker start psql
1jjcys9.explanation: exec starts a new process in an already running container. run creates a new container from an image.

gzvvad.text: How is a container fundamentally different from a virtual machine?
options: A container is slower than a VM
A VM has no isolation
A container always contains a full OS
A container shares the host OS kernel and isolates processes, while a VM emulates a full OS with its own kernel
gzvvad.explanation: That is why containers start in seconds and are lighter. The price: weaker isolation than a VM.

1obckvb.text: In docker compose there are the services app and db. How should app reach the database?
options: By the service name as the host: db:5432
By the host IP address 127.0.0.1:5432, as from the tests
localhost:5432, because all compose services run on one machine
1obckvb.explanation: Inside a container, localhost means the container itself. Compose creates a network where a service name resolves to its address. A classic cause of "works from the tests, doesn't from app".

w3wp6r.text: The error port is already allocated when starting a container. What do you do?
options: Run with sudo
Change the port inside the container, because PostgreSQL listens on 5432 by default and conflicts with any other service on the host
The host port is already taken by another process or container: free it or change the host port, for example -p 5433:5432
Reinstall Docker Desktop and reboot the computer to reset occupied ports
w3wp6r.explanation: Check docker ps for an old container. On Windows the port is often taken by a locally installed PostgreSQL.

tpbjgh.text: What does the -d flag do in docker compose up -d?
options: Removes the containers after they stop, like --rm in docker run
Starts the services in the background (detached) and returns the terminal
Downloads the images without starting containers and exits
Turns on debug mode with detailed logs for every service
tpbjgh.explanation: Without -d the logs of all services stream into the terminal, and Ctrl+C stops the stack.

ouyxgx.text: How is docker compose down different from docker compose down -v?
options: -v shows a detailed log of stopping each container and network
-v additionally removes volumes, that is, all the database data
No difference
-v only stops the containers without removing them, so they can be restarted
ouyxgx.explanation: For a clean test run down -v is useful. For keeping data between sessions it is dangerous.

1gqre7g.text: What is Docker's main benefit for QA?
options: Replacing test environments with production in a container, to test on real customer data without a separate environment
Speeding up the UI
A reproducible environment: the same versions of the database, services and browsers locally, for colleagues and on CI
Writing tests automatically from the services configuration in docker-compose.yml
1gqre7g.explanation: The "it works for me" argument disappears when everyone runs the same image. The official Playwright Docker image contains the needed browsers and system dependencies.

c3le85.text: Why does a Dockerfile first copy package.json, run npm ci, and only then COPY the rest of the code?
options: Because of layer caching: dependencies are reinstalled only when package.json changes, not on every code change
Dockerfile syntax requires it: COPY package.json must come before any other COPY
So that npm works without a network
To reduce the number of containers
c3le85.explanation: Every instruction creates a layer. If a layer hasn't changed, Docker takes it from the cache, so the order of instructions directly affects build speed on CI.

p1pzej.text: docker run postgres exits immediately. The most likely cause?
options: Postgres doesn't run in Docker without the -it and --privileged flags, because the database needs access to the host terminal
The port -p 5432:5432 is not specified, and the container exits because the database has nowhere to listen for connections
There is no -it flag, so the container gets no terminal and exits with code 0
The required POSTGRES_PASSWORD variable is not set, and docker logs will show a message about it
p1pzej.explanation: The official image requires a password or an explicit POSTGRES_HOST_AUTH_METHOD. The right way: docker run -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=secret -p 5432:5432 -d postgres:16.

1oeg0w5.text: How do error, defect and failure differ according to ISTQB?
options: An error is found by the tester while running tests, a defect is recorded by the developer in the code, and a failure is an incident record created by the support team
Error: visible incorrect behaviour. Defect: a human mistake. Failure: its consequence in code or a document
A failure is always in the code, a defect in the UI, and an error is the error message the user sees on screen
Error: a human mistake. Defect: its consequence in code or a document. Failure: visible incorrect behaviour during execution
1oeg0w5.explanation: Not every defect leads to a failure: code with a bug may never be executed.

17ndivi.text: What does the principle "exhaustive testing is impossible" mean?
options: Testing ends when the budget or time runs out, regardless of how many defects and risks were found
Automated tests cover everything, so exhaustiveness is achieved by automation, and manual testing only complements it
Only critical functions need to be tested, and the rest is left to users in production
Checking all combinations of inputs and states is unrealistic, so testing is based on risks and priorities
17ndivi.explanation: That is where test design techniques come from: they reduce the number of cases without a significant loss of coverage.

options: Most defects are concentrated in a small number of modules
Bugs always group in the UI layer, so regression starts from the interface
Identical bugs must be merged into a single report
Defects appear only during integration
1sov3sj.explanation: The practical conclusion: after a finding in a module it is worth digging deeper right there and strengthening regression around it.

bucrg.text: What does the "absence-of-errors fallacy" principle describe?
options: Testing proves there are no errors if all tests are green and coverage is 100%
There are no errors if all tests are green and requirements coverage is 100%, so the product can be released without further checks
Regression can be skipped
A system with no defects found may still be unfit if it doesn't meet the users' needs
bucrg.explanation: That is why validation (are we building the right product) is just as important as verification.

options: A report on the bugs found, with sprint metrics and a release recommendation
A list of test cases with priorities and the person responsible for each
A document about the scope, approach, resources, schedule, risks and the entry and exit criteria of testing
A checklist for smoke
d3jglw.explanation: A test strategy describes the general approach of an organisation or product, and a test plan makes it concrete for a release or project.

ucoxsw.text: How is a test case different from a checklist?
options: A checklist is more detailed: it has preconditions, steps and data, while a test case is a short list of what to check
Test cases are used only for automated tests in code, and checklists for manual checks, so manual teams don't write test cases at all
A checklist has preconditions, steps and expected result; a test case is a short list
A test case has preconditions, steps, data and expected result; a checklist is a short list of what to check
ucoxsw.explanation: A checklist is quicker to maintain and fits an experienced team. Test cases are needed for complex logic, regulatory requirements and onboarding.

options: A list of test environments and versions on which test cases are run
A table of links between requirements, test cases and defects that shows requirement coverage
A severity and priority matrix the tester uses with developers at the daily meeting to decide the order of fixing defects
A chart of test execution by sprint days with the people responsible
1g8pkri.explanation: It answers "which requirement nobody tested" and "which tests does a requirement change affect".

1j6gnaq.text: How is functional testing different from non-functional testing?
options: Non-functional testing is done only after release in production, because only there are the real load and users
It is the same thing according to ISTQB: both check the system's functions, and non-functional is just testing without documentation or customer requirements
Functional is manual and checks the UI, non-functional is automated and checks the API
Functional checks what the system does, non-functional checks how it does it: performance, security, usability, reliability
1j6gnaq.explanation: A transfer example: functionally, the money was debited correctly; non-functionally, the request was processed in 300 ms under load.

1660jig.text: How is exploratory testing different from ad hoc?
options: Exploratory has a goal, time boxes (sessions) and records its findings; ad hoc is completely unstructured
Exploratory is always automated with random data, and ad hoc is manual testing from a checklist
Ad hoc is used only for the UI, and exploratory only for APIs and integrations between services
Ad hoc has a goal and time boxes, exploratory is completely unstructured
1660jig.explanation: The session-based approach: a charter such as "explore transfers between currencies for 60 minutes", notes, bugs, questions.

options: Testing only security requirements and data leak risks
Skipping low-priority tests forever
Testing without documentation, where the tester decides what is risky
Prioritising tests by the probability of a defect and its impact on the business
ri2uir.explanation: For a bank, transfers and debits are higher risk than changing an avatar, so they get more coverage and automation.

options: Automated API tests that the customer runs before signing the acceptance act
Unit tests written by the customer to check the developers' code
Load testing the customer does before signing the acceptance act, to make sure the system will hold up in production
Acceptance testing by users or the customer: does the product solve their tasks
oc9q6m.explanation: UAT is usually the last stage before release and is done on an environment as close to production as possible.

1b5ahhp.text: How is alpha testing different from beta?
options: Beta is done by developers on their machines, and alpha by testers on a test environment
Alpha is automated, beta is manual
No difference in substance: alpha and beta are just iteration numbers of testing before release, like RC1 and RC2
Alpha is done inside the company, beta by real users in their own environment
1b5ahhp.explanation: Beta gives feedback on real data and devices that a test lab doesn't have.

lyuoi7.text: What is a blocker in a bug report?
options: A bug that blocks the developer, because they can't continue working on the task
A cosmetic defect
A defect that makes further testing or use of a key function impossible, with no workaround
Any bug with high priority that blocked the release
lyuoi7.explanation: For a blocker it is important to tell the team right away, not just file a ticket.

11hag43.text: A bug doesn't reproduce for the developer. What is most useful to add to the report?
options: Critical priority and a screenshot, so the developer picks the bug up faster
A link to the framework documentation and a description of how the feature should work, so the developer understands the expected behaviour
The exact environment, build, data, logs, HAR or a screen recording, and the reproduction rate
More emotion in the title and Critical priority, so the bug gets noticed
11hag43.explanation: "Can't reproduce" often means a difference in data or environment. The rate ("3 out of 10") hints at a race condition.

197zzri.text: What is the defect leakage metric?
options: The percentage of automated tests that failed on CI because of infrastructure problems, not defects in the app code
The speed at which the team closes bugs per sprint, in days
The share of defects missed by testing and found at a later stage or in production
The number of duplicate bugs filed by different testers
197zzri.explanation: A useful measure of testing effectiveness. It is important to analyse the cause of every leak, not just the number.

x77gh.text: How would you explain to a manager why 100% test case coverage doesn't guarantee quality?
options: Coverage shows what was checked, not how well: you can cover everything superficially and miss risky combinations, data and non-functional requirements
It does guarantee quality if the test cases are written from the requirements: then 100% coverage means all functions are checked and the product has no defects
Because automated tests are better than test cases, and real quality is guaranteed only by unit-test code coverage, not by cases
Because test cases go stale faster than they are updated, and coverage is always inaccurate
x77gh.explanation: The senior answer: coverage as a tool for finding gaps, not as a goal. Plus production metrics: leakage, incidents.

options: Testing two browsers in parallel with the same set of cases to compare results and find rendering differences
A technique that covers all pairs of parameter values with fewer tests than a full enumeration
Comparing two versions of a product with pairs of tests to find a regression between releases
Testing in pairs of testers, where one runs the steps and the other records the result
e4bzue.explanation: For 4 parameters with 3 values each, the full enumeration gives 81 combinations, pairwise about 9–10. Most defects come from the interaction of two parameters.

1f7x7l0.text: A password must be 8–20 characters. Which lengths do you check with boundary values (2 points)?
options: 0, 7, 21, 100 and an empty value
1f7x7l0.explanation: Plus separately an empty value and a very long one, but those are other classes.

options: Testing based on scenarios of the user's interaction with the system: the main flow and alternative ones
Testing classes and methods in code with unit scenarios
Performance testing of typical user scenarios under load
Testing boundaries and classes for each form field separately, without considering the sequence of the user's actions on the screen
19t0bfb.explanation: It is good at finding integration defects between steps that separate field checks miss.

options: Random clicking
Testing without requirements, where the tester guesses the expected result
Guessing the severity and priority of a bug without analysing the impact
A technique where tests are built on experience: where developers usually make mistakes
ng1cxr.explanation: Typical "guesses": empty values, spaces, special characters, time zones, double-clicking the pay button.

9j7vy.text: How is black box different from white box testing?
options: No difference: both test through the interface, and the name depends on whether the tester has seen the code at least once
White box is only for security and pentesting, black box for all other functionality
Black box is automatic, white box is manual
Black box tests behaviour without knowing the code, white box relies on the internal structure of the code
9j7vy.explanation: Grey box combines both: QA knows the architecture, the database and the API, but tests through the interface.

if8yg7.text: What are statement coverage and branch coverage?
options: Statement: the share of executed lines. Branch: the share of condition branches taken (true and false)
Statement: coverage of requirements by test cases. Branch: coverage of git branches by tests on CI
Statement: the share of condition branches taken. Branch: the share of executed lines
They are the same code coverage metric, counting the share of lines executed by tests, just in different tools
if8yg7.explanation: You can reach 100% statement coverage without taking any else branch, so branch coverage is stronger.

1bb4b3v.text: Discount: a VIP customer gets 10%, an amount over 1000 zł another 5%, a promo code another 5%. Which technique is best?
options: The pesticide paradox trap: check that discounts don't repeat across different cases
A decision table: 3 conditions give 8 combinations, each with the expected discount
Boundary values for each discount separately, without combinations
State transition
1bb4b3v.explanation: Plus boundary values for the amount: 999.99, 1000, 1000.01. Techniques are combined.

173k5pj.text: How do you test a transfer amount field with two decimal places?
options: Check only the UI mask of the field: if the mask doesn't accept letters and a third decimal place, backend checks are no longer needed
Check only the maximum and minimum amount, because the backend validation checks the other values automatically
Enter one valid amount and one too large, the backend checks the rest
Classes: valid, zero, negative, non-numeric, more than 2 decimals; limit boundaries; locale (comma and dot); rounding and float errors
173k5pj.explanation: The senior answer adds a backend check: bypassing the mask through the API, and that the debited amount equals the one shown.

1eor4u4.text: What is the Definition of Done?
options: The acceptance criteria of a specific story
The release date by which the team commits to finish all sprint tasks without exception
A team-agreed list of conditions for when a task is considered finished: code, review, tests, documentation
The list of sprint tasks the team took on during planning
1eor4u4.explanation: Acceptance criteria are specific to a story, while the DoD is shared by all tasks. QA should insist that automated tests are part of it.

qjeu5w.text: How are acceptance criteria different from test cases?
options: Test cases are shorter and describe only the positive scenario, while AC contain all the negative cases and boundary values
QA writes AC to verify, and the PO writes test cases as a description of business requirements
They are the same: AC are test cases, just in a different format
AC describe the conditions under which the story is accepted by the business; test cases check those conditions in detail and more
qjeu5w.explanation: Good AC are testable and unambiguous. The Given/When/Then format helps turn them into scenarios.

1805ipo.text: What does QA do at sprint planning?
options: Nothing: testing starts after development, so QA comes to the demo
Approves the release dates and the regression scope, while the other decisions on stories are made by developers without testing's participation
Only writes down the tasks assigned to them and waits for a build to test
Estimates the testing effort, asks questions about the requirements, points out risks and dependencies, and influences the story estimate
1805ipo.explanation: A story estimate that ignores testing and automation is systematically too low.

options: Release planning and distributing tasks for the next sprint
A meeting at the end of the sprint about the process: what worked, what didn't, what improvements to try
A product demo for the customer with a list of completed tasks
Analysing a specific bug
1ty8696.explanation: QA is well placed to bring facts: how many bugs came back, where builds were delayed.

options: Postponing bug fixes to the next release so as not to block the current deploy
Testing and monitoring in production: feature flags, canary releases, analysis of logs and metrics
Moving tests to the end of the sprint so developers have time to finish everything
Testing only the right panel of the UI and moving the rest to the end of the sprint
16zpkdf.explanation: It complements shift-left: it is impossible to reproduce all production conditions on a test environment.

eqj53h.text: At the end of the sprint 80% is done, and the release is tomorrow. What does a senior QA do?
options: Delays the release single-handedly, because they are responsible for product quality
Tests overnight alone to manage to check everything before the release, and doesn't tell the team about the risks so as not to disrupt the date
Assesses the risks of what is untested, gives the team facts and options (release behind a feature flag, without some features, postponing), and the decision is made together
Silently lets the release go, because the PO decides, and records the risks only at the retrospective
eqj53h.explanation: QA is not a "gatekeeper" but a source of information about risks. The main thing is to make the risk visible and record the decision.

d3y10y.text: What is technical debt in testing?
options: Open bugs in production that there was no time to fix
Outdated equipment and licences of test tools that the company hasn't updated for a long time and doesn't plan to
Accumulated compromises: flaky tests, outdated cases, manual regression instead of automation, which slow the team down
Open bugs in production that the team didn't manage to fix by the end of the quarter
d3y10y.explanation: Flaky tests that nobody trusts are worse than having none: the team gets used to ignoring a red pipeline.

19sjkw1.text: What is a feature flag and how does it affect testing?
options: A git branch where a new feature is developed before merging into main
A Jira label for tasks that go into the next release
A switch that turns a feature on without a new deploy; both states and the transition between them must be tested
A type of bug report in Jira for features that are temporarily turned off in production because of defects
19sjkw1.explanation: Combinations of several flags increase the number of configurations, so they should be removed after the full rollout.

a9xvk5.text: Where in DevTools do you see the status and body of an API response?
options: The Elements tab: select an element and look at the response property
The Sources tab: open api.js and find the server's response with the body and status in it
The Console tab: it shows all API responses with the body and status
The Network tab: select a request and look at Headers, Payload, Response
a9xvk5.explanation: From there you can also save a HAR to attach to the bug report and copy the request as cURL.

ugabca.text: How is localStorage different from sessionStorage and cookies?
options: It is the same storage with different APIs for convenience
Cookies are stored only on the server, localStorage in the browser, and sessionStorage is shared by all tabs
localStorage lives until cleared, sessionStorage until the tab is closed, and cookies are sent to the server with every request
sessionStorage is shared by all tabs and lives until the browser restarts, localStorage until the tab is closed, and cookies are not sent automatically
ugabca.explanation: When testing logout it is important to check that the tokens disappeared from all storages.

1y3ntsb.text: How do you check the page's behaviour on a slow connection?
options: Change the user agent to mobile, and the browser will slow the network down automatically
Network throttling in DevTools (for example Slow 3G) or emulation in automated tests
Open the page in incognito without a cache, because the browser then loads resources slower
Turn off the cache in DevTools so every request goes to the server
1y3ntsb.explanation: We look for: loaders, double clicks while waiting, timeouts, a broken layout without fonts.

12406il.text: How does testing on a mobile emulator in DevTools differ from a real device?
options: DevTools runs the real iOS WebKit engine in a Chrome window, so iPhone emulation fully matches a real device, including gestures and the keyboard
No difference: DevTools runs the real Safari engine for iPhone presets
An emulator is more accurate than a device, because it gives the same conditions to all testers
DevTools changes the size and user agent, but the engine stays desktop Chrome: Safari on iPhone, the keyboard, gestures and performance are different
12406il.explanation: Critical mobile scenarios need real devices or cloud farms (BrowserStack, Sauce Labs).

8kgcoh.text: The console shows "blocked by CORS policy". Whose bug is it and how do you check?
options: A browser bug that blocks requests to other domains, worked around by turning CORS off
Usually server configuration: the response lacks the required Access-Control-Allow-* headers; check the preflight OPTIONS in Network
The tester's mistake: CORS appears when the page is opened from localhost and disappears on the test environment, so no bug report is needed
A front-end markup bug: the form sends the request to the wrong domain
8kgcoh.explanation: Postman and curl don't enforce CORS, so "it works in Postman" doesn't disprove the bug.

1lck2rt.text: What is a HAR file and why put it in a bug report?
options: A server log with all the user's requests during a session
A recording of all the page's network requests and responses with timings, which the developer can examine on their side
A test case format for import into TestRail, containing steps, expected results and links to requirements
A screenshot of the page with the network requests highlighted
1lck2rt.explanation: A HAR may contain tokens and personal data: it must be sanitised before it is sent outside.

wqaeh7.text: How do you check that a button is usable from the keyboard?
options: Tab through: there is a visible focus, a logical order, and the button works on Enter or Space
Click with the mouse twice and check that the handler fired once
Look in the Console for JavaScript errors after clicking the button with the mouse
Check the button's colour and contrast against WCAG
wqaeh7.explanation: This is a basic accessibility check. A div with onclick and no tabindex or role is not reachable from the keyboard.

1vzd615.text: How can browser caching spoil the verification of a fix?
options: The cache is always off on test environments, so it has no effect
The browser shows an old version of JS or CSS, and it looks like the fix doesn't work; a hard refresh or Disable cache is needed
The browser clears the cache on every request, so it doesn't affect the check, and the problem is always in the server deploy
The cache affects only images and fonts, and JS is always downloaded again
1vzd615.explanation: Before Reopened, check the build version on the page or in Network to see that the file was downloaded again.

options: Deletes the old image and downloads a new one with the same tag
Downloads the image from the registry without starting a container
Updates a running container to version 16 without restarting
Starts a container from the image postgres:16
1k12cbj.explanation: docker run will pull the image itself if it is not present locally. A specific tag such as 16 is better than latest for reproducibility.

9e8is5.text: Why is the `latest` tag a poor fit for a test environment?
options: It can't be downloaded from Docker Hub without authorisation
It points to different versions at different times, so the environment stops being reproducible
It always points to the oldest stable version
It works only locally, and on CI Docker requires an explicit version number
9e8is5.explanation: Today's latest and latest a month from now may differ by a major version.

1jhq25i.text: What does the `EXPOSE 3000` instruction in a Dockerfile do?
options: Restricts incoming traffic to the given port in the Docker network
Sets the environment variable PORT=3000 for the app in the container
Opens port 3000 on the host for all network interfaces
Documents which port the container listens on, but by itself doesn't open it on the host
1jhq25i.explanation: To reach it from the host you need `-p 3000:3000` or ports in compose.

1ujax48.text: How is CMD different from ENTRYPOINT?
options: CMD sets the main command, ENTRYPOINT gives arguments that are easy to override
ENTRYPOINT sets the main command, CMD gives default arguments that are easy to override in docker run
CMD runs while the image is built, and ENTRYPOINT when the container starts
ENTRYPOINT can't be used together with CMD: Docker will take only the instruction described last
1ujax48.explanation: RUN runs during the build, and CMD and ENTRYPOINT when the container starts.

7m41up.text: How do you pass environment variables into a container in compose?
options: Through `environment:` or `env_file: .env` in the service
Through volumes
Only through the ENV instruction in the Dockerfile and rebuilding the image
Through `ports:`
7m41up.explanation: Secrets should not be written into docker-compose.yml in the repository.

x431wg.text: What does `depends_on` do in compose and what does it not guarantee?
options: Sets up a shared network between services and guarantees that the dependency is fully ready
Merges the services into one container and starts them in the given order
Guarantees full readiness of the service before the dependents start
Sets the start order, but without a healthcheck it doesn't guarantee the database is ready to accept connections
x431wg.explanation: The solution: a `healthcheck` in the db service and `depends_on: { db: { condition: service_healthy } }`.

options: Removes only container logs and temporary files, without touching images and networks
Updates all images to the latest versions and restarts the containers
Removes stopped containers, unused networks, dangling images and the build cache, freeing space
Restarts Docker and all containers with a clean state

A list of containers that compose doesn't start by default
The equivalent of .gitignore for volumes: files that are not kept between restarts
A list of files that don't go into the build context: node_modules, .git, reports

options: Building several images in parallel from one Dockerfile
Several FROM lines in one Dockerfile: the build happens in one image, and only the needed artifacts are copied into the final one
Starting a container in several stages: first dependencies, then the app, then the tests
A separate Dockerfile for each environment (dev, test, prod) with different base images
coqdpu.explanation: The final image is smaller and has no build tools, which is better for security and download speed.

1m7ej0t.text: How do you see the CPU and memory usage of containers?
options: `docker ps -a`
`docker logs`
`docker images`
`docker stats`
1m7ej0t.explanation: Useful when the test environment is slow: you can see which service eats the resources.

14ib3pe.text: How is WHERE different from HAVING?
options: WHERE filters rows before grouping, HAVING filters groups after GROUP BY
HAVING works only together with JOIN and filters the joined rows, while WHERE works only with one table without grouping
WHERE can't be used with GROUP BY
HAVING filters rows before grouping, WHERE filters groups after GROUP BY
14ib3pe.explanation: Aggregates such as COUNT(*) can be filtered only in HAVING, because at the WHERE stage the groups don't exist yet.

1iydso2.text: What will INNER JOIN of users and orders return?
options: All users, and for those with no orders the orders columns will be NULL
Only one row per user
Only the users who have at least one order (one row per order)
All orders, even those with no user, because INNER JOIN keeps the rows of the left orders table
1iydso2.explanation: INNER JOIN keeps the pairs for which the join condition holds. Users without orders drop out.

1q08et2.text: How do you find users with no orders at all?
options: u.id IS NULL
o.id IS NULL
o.user_id <> u.id
o.id = NULL
1q08et2.explanation: LEFT JOIN keeps all users, and for those with no orders the orders columns become NULL. A comparison with = NULL is never true.

1goxzvk.text: How is COUNT(*) different from COUNT(phone)?
options: COUNT(phone) counts unique values
COUNT(*) counts all rows, COUNT(phone) only the rows where phone is not NULL
COUNT(*) ignores NULL
COUNT(phone) counts all rows, COUNT(*) only the rows with no NULL in any column
1goxzvk.explanation: Unique values are counted by COUNT(DISTINCT phone). The difference between COUNT(*) and COUNT(col) shows how many NULLs the column has.

j8yyyf.text: How many rows will the query return if the table has rows with deleted_at = NULL?
options: 0: comparing with NULL gives UNKNOWN, you need IS NULL
A syntax error
All the rows of the table
All the rows with NULL: in PostgreSQL = NULL works like IS NULL
j8yyyf.explanation: NULL means "unknown", and any comparison with it using =, <> or > gives UNKNOWN. For checking there are IS NULL and IS NOT NULL.

1pn4r2r.text: In what order is a SELECT query logically executed?
options: FROM → SELECT → WHERE → HAVING
WHERE → FROM → SELECT → GROUP BY
FROM/JOIN → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY → LIMIT
SELECT → FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → ORDER BY → LIMIT, in the order of writing
1pn4r2r.explanation: That is why an alias from SELECT can't be used in WHERE (it doesn't exist yet), but can be used in ORDER BY.

gkdlva.text: How do you find duplicated emails?
options: SELECT email FROM users WHERE COUNT(email) > 1 GROUP BY email
SELECT email, COUNT(*) FROM users GROUP BY email HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
SELECT DISTINCT email, COUNT(email) FROM users WHERE COUNT(email) > 1 ORDER BY email
SELECT email FROM users ORDER BY email and look at which values stand next to each other, because duplicates follow one another after sorting
gkdlva.explanation: A classic interview task. WHERE with an aggregate gives an error; groups are filtered with HAVING.

1p5s8ci.text: How do DELETE, TRUNCATE and DROP differ?
options: TRUNCATE deletes the table
DROP deletes rows (can use WHERE), DELETE empties the whole table quickly, TRUNCATE deletes the table with its structure
DROP deletes only rows and keeps the structure, TRUNCATE deletes the table completely, and DELETE works only together with WHERE
DELETE deletes rows (can use WHERE), TRUNCATE empties the whole table quickly, DROP deletes the table together with its structure
1p5s8ci.explanation: In PostgreSQL TRUNCATE can also be rolled back within a transaction, but it doesn't fire ON DELETE triggers.

1smm27b.text: How is UNION different from UNION ALL?
options: UNION removes duplicates, UNION ALL keeps all rows and is faster
No difference in the result: both return all rows, but UNION ALL requires the same column names in all SELECTs
UNION ALL removes duplicates and is slower, UNION keeps all rows
UNION joins columns, UNION ALL joins rows
1smm27b.explanation: If duplicates can't occur or you need them, UNION ALL is cheaper: there is no sorting for deduplication.

ir0w9s.text: Salaries 100, 100, 90 in descending order. What do ROW_NUMBER, RANK and DENSE_RANK give?
ir0w9s.explanation: ROW_NUMBER is always unique. RANK gives equal ranks and skips the next number. DENSE_RANK has no gaps, so "the second highest salary" is DENSE_RANK = 2.

12ag57s.text: A transfer: debit account A and credit B. Which ACID property guarantees that only half of it is not executed?
options: Isolation
Atomicity
Durability
Consistency
12ag57s.explanation: Atomicity: either both changes are in the transaction or neither. Test: break the second update and check that A's balance didn't change.

options: A column that can't be NULL and has a unique value, which the database checks on every insert
A column that references the primary key of another table and doesn't allow saving a nonexistent reference
An index for fast search
A unique row identifier that the database generates automatically for each new record
12fiijr.explanation: Test: insert an order with a nonexistent user_id, and the DB must reject it. Deleting the parent row depends on ON DELETE (RESTRICT, CASCADE, SET NULL).

8161mj.text: Which column type is right for money amounts?
options: REAL
FLOAT or DOUBLE PRECISION, because they store fractional parts exactly down to the cent
NUMERIC/DECIMAL with fixed precision, or an integer in minor units
VARCHAR
8161mj.explanation: FLOAT stores a binary approximation: 0.1 + 0.2 doesn't equal 0.3. For financial data this is a schema defect worth raising.

19eubo5.text: Users: A has 2 orders, B has 1, C has none. How many rows does users LEFT JOIN orders return?
19eubo5.explanation: A gives 2 rows, B one, C one with NULL in place of the order. A LEFT JOIN on a 1:N relationship multiplies rows, so COUNT after a JOIN without DISTINCT often lies.

options: Rows 21 through 30
The first 30 rows
Rows 10 through 20 inclusive
Rows 20 through 30
1adg88e.explanation: Without ORDER BY the order is not guaranteed, and pagination may duplicate or lose rows. A typical pagination bug in an API.

hotax9.text: What will RIGHT JOIN of orders o with users u return?
options: A Cartesian product
All orders, even those without a user
Only the users who have at least one order, because RIGHT JOIN works like INNER
All users, and for those with no orders o.id will be NULL
hotax9.explanation: RIGHT JOIN is a mirrored LEFT JOIN. In practice it is rarely written: you swap the tables and use LEFT.

fv2f4t.text: When do you need FULL OUTER JOIN?
options: To join a table with itself
To remove duplicates after joining two tables and get only unique pairs of rows from both sides
To get rows from both tables, including those without a match on either side, for example to reconcile two data sets
To speed up a query on large tables, because it doesn't need indexes on the join keys
fv2f4t.explanation: A typical QA case: reconciling transactions from a bank statement and from the internal DB. Rows with NULL on one side are the discrepancies.

7p4jex.text: How many rows does a CROSS JOIN of tables with 3 and 4 rows give?
7p4jex.explanation: CROSS JOIN returns all combinations. A JOIN without an ON condition, or with a forgotten condition, gives the same explosion of rows.

2qvsv0.text: How do you get an employee together with the name of their manager from a single table employees(id, name, manager_id)?
options: A self-join: `FROM employees e LEFT JOIN employees m ON m.id = e.manager_id`
You need a separate managers table
A UNION of two SELECTs
`SELECT name, manager_id FROM employees`
2qvsv0.explanation: LEFT, so as not to lose the director who has no manager. Aliases are mandatory because the table is the same.

785ylf.text: Why doesn't this query return users without orders?
options: A WHERE condition on the right table discards the rows with NULL and effectively turns LEFT JOIN into INNER
Because of a syntax error: LEFT JOIN can't be combined with WHERE on columns of the right table
LEFT JOIN doesn't work with WHERE
Because status must be in SELECT
785ylf.explanation: To keep all users, move the condition into ON: `LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.user_id = u.id AND o.status = 'PAID'`.

16v33zz.text: After JOIN of orders and payments the order total came out twice as large. The most likely cause?
options: A wrong column type
DISTINCT is needed in SUM: `SUM(DISTINCT amount)` removes duplicates and returns the right order total
A 1:N relationship with payments multiplies the order rows; aggregate separately in subqueries or CTEs
A bug in the SUM function: it counts NULL as the sum of the previous row, so COALESCE is needed
16v33zz.explanation: Fan-out after a JOIN is the classic cause of "wrong" reports. SUM(DISTINCT amount) is not a solution: equal amounts from different orders would collapse.

14d9a7q.text: What will the query return if blocked_users.user_id has at least one NULL?
options: A runtime error, because PostgreSQL doesn't allow NULL in a subquery result for the NOT IN operator
No rows at all: a comparison with NULL gives UNKNOWN, and NOT IN never becomes true
All the non-blocked users, and the rows with NULL are simply skipped
All users
14d9a7q.explanation: The safe variant: `NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM blocked_users b WHERE b.user_id = u.id)`. A classic interview trap.

n29n3h.text: How is EXISTS different from IN?
options: EXISTS checks that a correlated subquery has at least one row and works correctly with NULL in NOT EXISTS
EXISTS returns the value of the first row found, IN returns a boolean for each row
IN is always faster
They are synonyms with the same NULL behaviour: the only difference is that EXISTS is faster on large tables
n29n3h.explanation: Modern optimisers often plan IN and EXISTS the same way. The main difference in practice: how NOT IN behaves with NULL.

options: An index that PostgreSQL temporarily creates for a query with WITH and drops after it runs
A named temporary result within a single query, which makes complex queries readable
A trigger
A stored table that exists until the end of the session and is available to other queries
6i3ojg.explanation: A CTE exists only while the query runs. For reuse across queries you need a view.

options: For parallel execution
For walking hierarchies: a category tree, a chain of managers, a referral graph
For re-running a query in a loop on a schedule without an external scheduler
For recursively dropping tables
1if1plw.explanation: A recursive CTE has a base part and a recursive part joined by UNION ALL, and it stops when the recursive part returns nothing.

n0y80.text: How do you find orders with an amount greater than the average?
options: `SELECT * FROM orders HAVING amount > AVG(amount)`
`SELECT * FROM orders WHERE amount > (SELECT AVG(amount) FROM orders)`
`SELECT * FROM orders GROUP BY amount > AVG(amount)`
`SELECT * FROM orders WHERE amount > AVG(amount) OVER ()`: a window function computes the average over the whole table
n0y80.explanation: An aggregate can't be used directly in WHERE, so the average is computed with a scalar subquery.

1w1w7s3.text: What does `SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY account_id ORDER BY created_at)` compute?
options: A running balance for each account separately in chronological order
An error: SUM can't be used with OVER
The sum of only the last row of each account, repeated for all that account's transactions
The total across all accounts, repeated in every row
1w1w7s3.explanation: Unlike GROUP BY, a window function doesn't collapse rows: every transaction stays a separate row with the balance at that moment.

1vdqvwh.text: What does `LAG(balance) OVER (ORDER BY created_at)` do?
options: Returns the balance value from the previous row in the given order
Sorts in descending order
Returns the balance value from the next row in the given order
Computes the average balance for the previous day in chronological order
1vdqvwh.explanation: LAG and LEAD are handy for checks: the difference between neighbouring balances must equal the transaction amount.

121hy1h.text: How do you select the last transaction of each account?
options: `DISTINCT account_id, created_at`
`SELECT * FROM transactions ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 1` for each account separately in one query
`ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY account_id ORDER BY created_at DESC)` in a CTE and a filter `rn = 1`
`SELECT * FROM transactions GROUP BY account_id HAVING created_at = MAX(created_at)`
121hy1h.explanation: PostgreSQL also has `DISTINCT ON (account_id) ... ORDER BY account_id, created_at DESC`.

cvas9r.text: Why can't you write `WHERE ROW_NUMBER() OVER (...) = 1`?
options: It is allowed if you specify PARTITION BY in OVER
Because ROW_NUMBER returns text, and WHERE in PostgreSQL compares only numbers with numbers
Because HAVING is needed
Window functions are computed after WHERE, so you filter in an outer query or a CTE
cvas9r.explanation: The logical order: FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, windows, SELECT, ORDER BY.

options: The first value that is not NULL
The last non-empty value
NULL if at least one field is NULL
The concatenation of all the fields
To replace a NULL denominator with 0 and avoid an empty result
To speed up the query
To avoid division by zero: at 0 the denominator becomes NULL, and the result is NULL too
To round the division result to an integer and remove the fractional part from percentages
m7pk0q.explanation: `paid_count * 100.0 / NULLIF(total_count, 0)` won't fail with a division by zero error.

options: 2.5: PostgreSQL automatically converts the division result to numeric
2: division of integers gives an integer
An error: an explicit CAST to numeric is needed
1dx6clo.explanation: For a fractional result at least one operand must be numeric: `5 / 2.0` or `5::numeric / 2`.

15m3e1v.text: What will `'Hello ' || NULL` return in PostgreSQL?
options: 'Hello NULL'
An error
NULL
'Hello '
15m3e1v.explanation: The || operator with NULL gives NULL. The function `concat('Hello ', NULL)` ignores NULL and returns 'Hello '.

6ac5d1.text: How do you search emails case-insensitively in PostgreSQL?
options: `WHERE email LIKE 'ANNA@%'`, because LIKE in PostgreSQL is case-insensitive
`WHERE email = 'anna@%'`
`WHERE email ILIKE 'anna@%'` or `WHERE lower(email) = lower($1)`
`WHERE CASE email`
6ac5d1.explanation: ILIKE is specific to PostgreSQL. For fast search, a functional index on lower(email) is created.

1pwqmar.text: How do you group transactions by day?
options: `GROUP BY created_at` with `ORDER BY created_at`
`GROUP BY DAY(created_at)` with `ORDER BY DAY(created_at)`
`GROUP BY date_trunc('day', created_at)` or `created_at::date`
`ORDER BY created_at`
1pwqmar.explanation: Grouping by the full timestamp gives a group for every millisecond. Mind the time zone: a day in UTC and a day in Warsaw are different.

epk5dm.text: How do you select orders from the last 7 days?
options: `WHERE DAY(created_at) < 7 AND MONTH(created_at) = MONTH(now())`
`WHERE created_at BETWEEN 0 AND 7`
`WHERE created_at > now() - 7`
`WHERE created_at >= now() - interval '7 days'`
epk5dm.explanation: For tests it is better to fix the date in the query rather than depend on now(), otherwise results depend on when it runs.

rg3f5m.text: How do you output the status "large" for amounts over 10,000 and "regular" for the rest?
options: `DECODE(amount)`
`SWITCH amount WHEN > 10000 THEN 'large' DEFAULT 'regular' END`
`CASE WHEN amount > 10000 THEN 'large' ELSE 'regular' END`
`IF(amount > 10000, 'large', 'regular')` in PostgreSQL
rg3f5m.explanation: IF as a function exists in MySQL; in PostgreSQL you use CASE.

l6vbb7.text: What is `AVG(rating)` for the values 5, NULL, 3?
options: NULL
4: AVG ignores NULL
2.67: NULL is counted as 0
l6vbb7.explanation: If NULL should mean 0, you need `AVG(COALESCE(rating, 0))`. That is a business decision, not a technical one.

i3g4ar.text: What will `SUM(amount)` return for a table with no rows?
options: An error
NULL
An empty string
i3g4ar.explanation: COUNT(*) on an empty table gives 0, while SUM, AVG and MAX give NULL. In reports this often gives an "empty cell" instead of 0.

ofrvjl.text: Where will NULLs be with `ORDER BY paid_at ASC` in PostgreSQL?
options: At the end: by default NULLs are considered larger than any value
At the start: NULLs are considered smaller than any value
They are not returned, because ORDER BY automatically discards rows with NULL in the sort column
Randomly, depending on the order the rows are written on disk
ofrvjl.explanation: For DESC the NULLs come first. Explicit control: `NULLS FIRST` or `NULLS LAST`.

h8259x.text: How do you count the number of unique customers who paid?
options: `SELECT UNIQUE(user_id) FROM payments`
`SELECT COUNT(user_id) FROM payments GROUP BY user_id`
`SELECT DISTINCT COUNT(user_id) FROM payments`
`SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) FROM payments`
h8259x.explanation: DISTINCT COUNT(...) counts all rows, and DISTINCT is applied to the single result number.

17y8sc9.text: What happens after `UPDATE accounts SET balance = 0;`?
options: The first row is updated
Nothing: PostgreSQL blocks UPDATE without WHERE and returns an error
All the rows of the table are updated
A syntax error
17y8sc9.explanation: That is why changes on shared environments are made in a transaction: BEGIN, UPDATE, check the number of changed rows, then COMMIT or ROLLBACK.

agm83v.text: How do you get the id of the just inserted row in PostgreSQL?
options: `SELECT MAX(id) FROM users` right after the insert in the same session
`INSERT INTO users (email) VALUES ('a@b.c') RETURNING id`
`LAST_INSERT_ID()`
`SELECT @@IDENTITY`
agm83v.explanation: MAX(id) is unreliable with concurrent inserts. RETURNING is atomic.

options: Ignores duplicates by email: if the row already exists, the insert is skipped without changes
An upsert: inserts the row, and on a conflict on the unique email updates name with the value from the new insert
Throws an error on a duplicate
Deletes the old row with this email and inserts a new one, so the user's id changes to a new value
13ye67x.explanation: Handy for idempotent seeding of test data. To ignore conflicts there is `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING`.

1daas27.text: Why is `ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN phone text NOT NULL` risky on a table with data?
options: It isn't
Existing rows have no value, so without DEFAULT the command fails
It will lock the table forever
It will delete the existing rows without a phone value to satisfy the NOT NULL constraint
1daas27.explanation: Options: add it with a DEFAULT, or add it nullable, fill it in, and only then set NOT NULL.

sd9xrx.text: What is the CHECK constraint for?
options: Logs changes
Creates an index on balance and checks the column type on every insert
The DB will reject any update that makes the balance negative
Checks the type of the balance column on every insert
sd9xrx.explanation: Test: try to debit more than there is through the API. Even if the backend lets it through, the database must reject it, and it shows up as a 500 instead of a 4xx.

ru5d7k.text: What does ON DELETE CASCADE do?
options: Sets NULL in the child rows that reference the deleted parent row
Forbids deleting the parent row while child rows exist
When the parent row is deleted, automatically deletes the child rows that reference it
Archives the rows
ru5d7k.explanation: For financial data a cascading delete is dangerous: deleting a customer would delete their transactions. Soft delete is often used.

4rgvym.text: What is the default isolation level in PostgreSQL?
options: Repeatable Read
Serializable
Read Uncommitted
Read Committed
4rgvym.explanation: In PostgreSQL Read Uncommitted behaves like Read Committed: there are no dirty reads at all.

options: A lost update: the second transaction overwrites the first one's changes in the same row
Reading data that another transaction changed but hasn't committed yet
Reading from a dropped table
A repeated query in a transaction returns new rows that another transaction inserted and committed
19cjw25.explanation: A non-repeatable read is about a change to an already read row, a phantom is about new rows appearing for the same condition.

14atwjc.text: Two parallel transfers read a balance of 100, each debits 80 and writes 20. What is this problem called?
options: Deadlock: two transactions block each other, and the database aborts both
Lost update: the second update overwrites the first, and 160 is debited from a balance of 100
Dirty read
Phantom read: the second transaction sees the first one's new rows
14atwjc.explanation: Solutions: an atomic `UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 80 WHERE id = $1 AND balance >= 80`, SELECT FOR UPDATE, or a higher isolation level. QA catches this with parallel requests.

1kz1l85.text: What happens on a deadlock in PostgreSQL?
options: The server restarts
Both transactions wait forever until an administrator aborts one of them
The database detects the mutual lock and aborts one of the transactions with an error
Both commit
1kz1l85.explanation: The application must handle the error and retry the transaction. Test: parallel transfers A→B and B→A.

options: Saves the database to disk and creates a backup of the current state
Creates a point in a transaction to which you can roll back without cancelling the whole transaction
Creates a backup
Closes the transaction and saves all changes to disk, like COMMIT
5uxrub.explanation: `ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT s1` cancels changes after the point, and the rest of the transaction continues.

1yenqxh.text: How can tests clean up their data using transactions?
options: COMMIT after every test and drop the tables in afterAll
Delete the whole database after every test and restore from a backup before the next one
Open a transaction before the test and roll it back afterwards, if the test and the app share one connection
It is impossible
1yenqxh.explanation: For e2e through the UI this usually doesn't work: the app has its own connections. Then unique data per test and cleanup through the API help.

16jxqec.text: What is the price of an index?
options: It speeds up reads by the column, but slows down INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE and takes space
There is no price: an index speeds up all operations, so it is put on every column
It locks the table
It slows down reads
16jxqec.explanation: That is why indexes are added for real queries, not on every column.

otzl6q.text: Will an ordinary B-tree index be used for the condition `WHERE email LIKE '%@bank.test'`?
options: Yes, if the table is small
Only with ILIKE
Yes, always: a B-tree index suits any LIKE pattern
No: a pattern with % at the start doesn't allow a prefix search
otzl6q.explanation: `LIKE 'anna%'` can use an index (with a suitable opclass or the C locale). For searching in the middle of a string there are pg_trgm trigram indexes.

options: No difference: both run the query, ANALYZE only formats the output
EXPLAIN shows the plan without running, EXPLAIN ANALYZE actually runs the query and shows the real time
ANALYZE updates the table statistics without running the query, and EXPLAIN shows the actual execution time
EXPLAIN runs the query twice and shows the average time, and EXPLAIN ANALYZE only builds the plan without running the query
1ri7huk.explanation: Careful: `EXPLAIN ANALYZE DELETE ...` really deletes the data. On shared environments wrap it in a transaction with ROLLBACK.

1doxx85.text: What does Seq Scan mean in a query plan on a large table?
options: The query ran in parallel
The query used an index to read sorted data sequentially
The database reads the whole table row by row: often a sign of a missing or unused index
The query is cached, and the database returns the result from memory without reading the table
1doxx85.explanation: On small tables a Seq Scan is normal and even faster than an index.

1c4tnk.text: What does PostgreSQL create automatically for PRIMARY KEY and UNIQUE?
options: Nothing: indexes are always created by hand
A trigger
A separate table
A unique index
1c4tnk.explanation: An index is not created automatically for foreign keys, which is a frequent cause of slow JOINs and DELETEs.

m14vak.text: What does the table orders(id, user_id, user_email, user_name, amount) violate?
options: The PRIMARY KEY constraint
Third normal form: email and name depend on user_id, not on the order's id
Nothing: denormalisation is always correct for order tables in fintech
First normal form, because a row stores data of two entities
m14vak.explanation: The consequence: changing an email in users won't update old orders. Sometimes this is deliberate (a snapshot of data at the time of purchase), and then it is worth documenting.

1n4fu9.text: What does first normal form require?
options: Only numeric keys
Foreign keys and no NULL in any column
No NULL in columns and a primary key in every table
Atomic values in cells, with no comma-separated lists and no repeating groups of columns
1n4fu9.explanation: A column `phones = '123, 456'` violates 1NF and complicates search and validation.

18lswu5.text: How is a view different from a materialized view?
options: No difference: both store the result and update automatically
A materialized view updates automatically on every table change, and a regular view caches the result until REFRESH
A view runs the query on every access, a materialized view stores the result and needs REFRESH
A view stores data on disk
18lswu5.explanation: When testing reports on a materialized view remember: fresh data appears only after REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW.

118x35x.text: Why use `timestamptz` rather than `timestamp` for operation times in fintech?
options: timestamptz stores a moment in time in UTC and converts it correctly to the session's time zone; a timestamp without a zone is ambiguous
No difference: both types store the time in the database server's zone, and timestamptz only shows the zone in the output
timestamptz takes less space and stores a date without time, while timestamp stores date and time together with the server's zone
timestamp doesn't store seconds and milliseconds, while timestamptz does
118x35x.explanation: Daylight-saving bugs and "a day in Kyiv versus a day in Warsaw" often have their root exactly here.

1qhcql4.text: How do you check through the DB that an API transfer was processed correctly?
options: Find the transaction by the id from the response and check the amount, status, currency, both accounts and that other rows are unchanged
Look at COUNT(*) in the transactions table before and after the request
Check the UI
Check only the API response: if the status is 201, the data in the database is guaranteed to be correct, because the same service wrote it
1qhcql4.explanation: Checking that "nothing extra changed" is just as important as checking the expected changes.

1epvut5.text: How do you test a search field for SQL injection?
options: Check the case of the entered text and the field length, because injections work only with uppercase SQL commands
Turn off JavaScript
Enter a very long string and check that the field truncates it to the character limit
Enter `' OR '1'='1` or a single quote and check that there is no SQL error, no extra data and no 500; the right defence is parameterised queries
1epvut5.explanation: SQL error text appearing in the response is already a security defect: it reveals the DB structure.

1ceflpa.text: Which HTTP methods are idempotent according to the specification?
options: POST, PUT, PATCH, because they change data, and GET and DELETE don't
Only GET
GET, PUT, DELETE (and also HEAD, OPTIONS)
GET, POST, PUT (and also PATCH), because a repeat always gives the same status
1ceflpa.explanation: Idempotent means that repeating the same request doesn't change the result after the first execution. POST is not idempotent: two identical POSTs create two resources. PATCH is not guaranteed to be idempotent.

options: 401: the server doesn't know who you are (no token or an invalid one). 403: it knows, but you have no rights
401 for GET, 403 for POST
401: the server knows who you are, but you have no rights. 403: no token or an invalid one
They are synonyms: both mean no access, and the choice depends only on the backend framework and its settings
hggemm.explanation: 401 Unauthorized effectively means "not authenticated". 403 Forbidden means "authenticated, but access is forbidden". Check both scenarios separately.

52wcpq.text: Which status is expected after a successful POST that created a resource?
options: 204 No Content
201 Created, often with a Location header or an id in the body
200 OK with the created resource in the body, because 201 is used only for PUT
Always 202 Accepted
52wcpq.explanation: 201 shows the resource was created. 202 fits when processing is asynchronous, for example a transfer in the PENDING status. 204 means success with no body.

i0yg1j.text: How is PUT different from PATCH?
options: PUT replaces the resource entirely, PATCH changes only the passed fields
PATCH replaces the resource entirely, PUT changes only the passed fields
No difference, they are synonyms
PATCH is always idempotent and creates the resource if it doesn't exist, while PUT is never idempotent
i0yg1j.explanation: Test case: PUT without one field. By the standard the field must be reset or a validation error returned. If the behaviour is like PATCH, it is a deviation from the contract worth recording.

1vdy74t.text: The request GET /users/42?active=true. Which is the path parameter and which is the query?
options: 42 is a query parameter because it is numeric, and active=true is path because it sets a resource filter
active=true is a path parameter, 42 is a query parameter
Both are query parameters, because everything after the domain name is passed in the query string
42 is a path parameter, active=true is a query parameter
1vdy74t.explanation: The path identifies the resource, the query filters, sorts or paginates. An invalid path often gives 404, an invalid query usually 400.

tpom5y.text: The API returns 500 for an invalid request body. Is that a bug?
options: No: 500 fits any processing error, as long as the body has a description
Yes. A client error must give a 4xx with a description, and 500 means an unhandled exception on the server
Only for GET: for POST, PUT and PATCH, 500 on an invalid body is considered the norm by the HTTP specification
No, if the response body has the error text: the client will read the message, and the status code no longer matters
tpom5y.explanation: 500 on incorrect input means the server doesn't validate data and crashes. Expected is 400 or 422 with a message saying which field is wrong.

10nxca2.text: A 200 OK response with the body {"error": "Insufficient funds"}. How do you assess it?
options: Fine: the status describes the transport, and business errors are passed in the body with 200 by the REST standard
It is a contract defect: the error must have a matching 4xx status, because clients and monitoring go by the code
A bug only in the UI
Fine for fintech: payment APIs under the PSD2 standard always return 200 and pass business errors in the body
10nxca2.explanation: The client, retries, alerts and logs look at the status. A 200 with an error in the body hides failures. For insufficient funds 422 or 409 fit, by agreement.

pabqvn.text: User A requests GET /orders/123, which belongs to user B, and gets the data. What is this?
options: Normal behaviour if A is logged in and the request has a valid token
A CDN caching bug, through which the user got someone else's cached response
A performance problem
IDOR (Broken Object Level Authorization), a critical security defect
pabqvn.explanation: The server checked authentication but not the resource owner. Expected is 403 or 404. The check: two users, swapping ids between them.

4rap2o.text: Why do payment APIs have the Idempotency-Key header?
options: For caching the response in the browser
So that repeating the same request (a retry after a timeout) doesn't create a second payment
For authorising the payment instead of a token, so Bearer isn't passed in every request
For encrypting the payment body with the client's key, so the bank can verify the integrity of the request
4rap2o.explanation: Test: two identical POSTs with one key must give one operation, and the second gets the same response. The same key with a different body must give an error.

1f1gium.text: How is Content-Type different from Accept?
options: Content-Type describes the format of the body being sent, Accept says which format the client wants to receive
Accept describes the format of the request body, Content-Type is only for the server's response, and the client doesn't send it at all
Accept describes the format of the body being sent, Content-Type says which format the client wants to receive
Content-Type sets the encoding of the token in Authorization, and Accept the response language for localisation
1f1gium.explanation: Negative cases: a wrong Content-Type (415 Unsupported Media Type is expected) and an unsupported Accept (406 Not Acceptable).

yh3hov.text: Registration with an email that already exists. Which status is the most logical?
options: 404 Not Found
200 OK
409 Conflict
500 Internal Server Error
yh3hov.explanation: 409 means a conflict with the state of the resource. Some teams return 400 or 422; the main thing is that it is in the contract and is not a 2xx or 5xx.

options: A server timeout: the request is being processed longer than the gateway allows
Payment required: API access ended because of the plan limit
Too Many Requests: a rate limit kicked in, often with a Retry-After header
The request is too large to process, so the server asks to split it into parts
p19bu6.explanation: For login and OTP a rate limit is a security requirement. Check that the limit fires and that access is restored after a pause.

2lwh22.text: The variable baseUrl is set in the Environment and in the Collection with different values. Which will Postman take?
options: Environment: the narrower scope overrides the wider one (Local > Data > Environment > Collection > Global)
Collection: it is closer to the request and overrides the environment (Global > Collection > Environment > Data > Local)
The one created first
Always Global
2lwh22.explanation: The priority goes from the narrowest scope to the widest. So a "foreign" variable in the environment can silently override the collection's value.

1bd62ev.text: What does it mean that HTTP is stateless?
options: The server doesn't remember previous requests; each request carries everything needed (token, cookie)
The server has no database and stores no data between requests
Responses can't be cached, because each request is processed anew without saving the result
Requests go without headers
1bd62ev.explanation: User state lives in a token, a cookie or the DB, not in the connection. Hence the test cases for an expired and a revoked token.

9a158z.text: What does JSON Schema validation of a response check?
options: The structure: presence of fields, their types, required fields, allowed values
The response status code and the server's response time for each request
Specific business data values: amounts, statuses and dates match the expected ones
Response time
9a158z.explanation: A schema catches a broken contract: a field disappeared, a type changed from number to string. Specific values are checked with separate assertions.

options: The request was accepted for processing, but the result will come later
An empty request without a body, which the server rejected
Success with no response body, typical for DELETE or PUT
The resource was not found, but the request was correct
xsce8a.explanation: Test: after a 204 the body must be empty, and a repeated GET of the resource must give 404 (for DELETE).

options: When the response is cached by a proxy and returned to the client without reaching the backend, to reduce load
When the resource was created and its id is returned in the Location header
When the request was accepted but processing is asynchronous: a transfer is queued, a report is being generated
When the request was rejected by validation, but the server doesn't want to reveal the reason
m7mtws.explanation: Then the status is checked by polling GET or a webhook. The test must wait for the final state, not only check 202.

options: 422 is for server-side database validation errors, and 400 for any client errors, including authorisation
422: the request is syntactically incorrect (broken JSON). 400: the format is right, but the data fails validation
400 is used only for GET requests with wrong parameters, and 422 for any errors in the body of POST, PUT and PATCH
400: the request is syntactically incorrect (broken JSON). 422: the format is right, but the data fails validation
ool2bg.explanation: Many APIs return 400 for both cases. The main thing is that the behaviour matches the contract and the body explains the error.

1pvwa1.text: DELETE on `/api/accounts` (the collection) returns 405. What does it mean?
options: The server is unavailable
No permission to delete: an admin role is needed, and the server returns 405 instead of 403 for security reasons
The resource was not found at this path, so the server can't determine the method
The method is not allowed for this resource; the Allow header should list the permitted methods
1pvwa1.explanation: 405 is better than 404 or 500 in this case: the client understands that the resource exists but doesn't support the method.

6abq7t.text: What does 415 Unsupported Media Type mean?
options: The client doesn't accept the response format given in the Accept header
The body is too large
The server doesn't accept the body format given in Content-Type
Wrong URL encoding
6abq7t.explanation: Negative test: send JSON with `Content-Type: text/plain`. For a response the client doesn't accept there is 406.

options: A URL with parameters that is too long for the server to handle
Too many requests from one client per minute
The request body is too large: for example, a file over the upload limit
A request processing timeout: the server didn't respond in the allotted time and dropped the connection
5n4seg.explanation: A limit boundary test: a file exactly at the limit, a byte over, and a check that the server doesn't fail with a 500.

options: 502 and 504 are client errors of a wrong request through a gateway, and 503 means the server rejected the request for lack of authorisation
502: the service is temporarily unavailable. 503: the gateway didn't wait for a response. 504: the gateway got an invalid response
All three mean an error in the application code, and the difference is only in which programming language the backend uses
502: the gateway got an invalid response from the service. 503: the service is temporarily unavailable. 504: the gateway didn't wait for a response
1kef5h8.explanation: For QA it is a hint where to look: 504 often means a slow query to the DB or a third-party provider.

options: 307 is a permanent redirect that the browser caches forever, and 302 is temporary, and both keep the request method
302 has no Location header and just reloads the current page, while 307 redirects to a new address with Location
302 guarantees the method and body are preserved, and 307 always turns POST into GET
307 guarantees that the method and body are preserved on redirect, while 302 historically allowed clients to change POST to GET
7yysdn.explanation: The permanent equivalents: 301 and 308. For a POST after payment the method on redirect is critical.

1wre745.text: What is the HEAD method for?
